title: TauricResearch - Trading Agents
author: pigorg01
selftext:
Hi everyone.

I’m testing this software. It allows for a mix of technical and fundamental analysis on individual stocks.

So far, I’ve tested it using the paid version of Claude, but I was thinking of switching to a free AI or something like:

\- Ollama

\- Google Gemini

It’s quite resource-intensive. Using Sonnet to analyze a single stock costs around $2, while using Haiku costs about $1.

Keep in mind that a lot of the work involves web research (scraping-style), so Haiku might actually be sufficient.

Since the software analyzes one stock at a time, I was thinking of creating a second agent to first screen for the best stocks—or perhaps those I deem best based on specific parameters—and then pass that data to the main agent for an in-depth analysis.

What do you think? Is this a sound approach?

Thanks.

replies.author: pigorg01
replies.body:
My idea is to work with three agents in sequence:

\----> Agent 1: I want to scan 50–100 titles for an initial screening. I think using optimized filters would suffice, though one could also use Ollama—a free AI that runs locally—if desired.  
\->I extract 5 titles.

\----> Agent 2 (Deep Analysis): Here, I would use Tavily Research combined with Claude Sonnet.  
\->I analyze the 5 titles and generate a report for each.

\----> Agent 3: Compares the 5 completed reports and makes a selection. A free, locally hosted AI like Ollama should work well for this step.

That is the basic concept.

comments.author: llmops_engineer
comments.body:
yeah, the screener → analyzer pattern is solid. we run something similar for financial document analysis, and the cost difference between "analyze everything with sonnet" vs "haiku for triage, sonnet for deep dive" is usually 4-5x.



a few things we learned:



1) haiku is fine for screening if the criteria are mostly structured (PE ratio < 15, revenue growth > 10%, etc). but if your screener needs to parse earnings calls or news sentiment, haiku starts hallucinating or missing nuance. we use sonnet 3.5 for screening when the criteria involve text understanding, haiku only for pure numerical filters.



2) $1-2 per stock analysis is expensive at scale. if you're analyzing 50 stocks/week, that's $200-400/month just for inference. a few optimizations that cut our costs by 60%:

   \- cache analysis results with a TTL (stock fundamentals don't change daily)

   \- batch similar analyses together (same sector, same time period) so context can be reused

   \- use structured outputs (JSON mode) instead of parsing free text — fewer retries, lower token count



3) ollama for screening can work, but expect 30-50% accuracy drop on complex reasoning tasks. we tested llama 3.1 8B vs haiku for financial screening — llama missed 40% of the red flags that haiku caught. fine for rough filtering, but you'll need sonnet/opus for the final pass.



4) the two-agent approach you're describing (screener → analyzer) is exactly right, but add a third layer: a "validator" agent that spot-checks 10% of the analyzer's outputs against ground truth. catches drift early before it compounds.



on the web scraping bottleneck: if most of the cost is from fetching + parsing web content, consider a lightweight preprocessing step with a cheaper model (haiku or even gemini flash) to extract structured data first, then pass clean JSON to the analyzer. cuts context length by 70%, which cuts cost proportionally.



what's your target volume? 10 stocks/week or 500? the architecture changes a lot based on that.

replies.author: pigorg01
replies.body:
My plan is to cover 50 stocks per week. I’m considering an initial screening process focused on:

\- large-cap stocks

\- stocks with strong fundamentals

\- stocks that have experienced a significant drawdown over the last 6 months



I was thinking of using Ollama for this preliminary analysis.



Then, I would pass the stocks selected by Ollama—5 per day (or up to 10 per week, given that I want to do swing trading)—to the second agent (Sonnet) for analysis.



Finally, I would pass them to the third agent (Sonnet), which would objectively determine which stocks meet the right criteria.



However, I’ve noticed that Sonnet consumes a lot of resources, so I need to estimate the weekly costs first.
